beats.narration_text: The obvious guess is that Claude approves your leave request — the way a manager would. Wrong branch. It's running a written policy check. So what's actually on that check?

beats.narration_text: A Skill isn't a plugin or an API — it's a folder. This one's called leave-tracker, and inside it is a single file, SKILL.md, written in plain English. That file is the whole program: the rules, the order, what to flag. The choice is deliberate — text you can read is text you can audit. No hidden logic sitting where the reviewer can't see it.

props.title: A skill is a folder.
props.calloutText: The SKILL.md is the instruction set.

beats.narration_text: The pipeline lives in a Steps section — a numbered list Claude runs top to bottom. Read the file, apply each step to your request, return the result. No branching, no jumping ahead, unless a step itself says otherwise. What that buys you is repeatability — the same request fed in twice goes through the same list, and the list can't quietly change its mind between runs.

Here's what's actually happening on each item. Check the requested or logged absence against three things the file spells out — the accrual rules, the eligibility windows, and the blackout dates — and flag anything that doesn't line up. The design choice is to stay inside the written policy and only the written policy. What that costs you is judgment calls the policy didn't foresee. What you get is the same shape of report every time, from a check you can read line by line before you trust it.

props.heading: The interesting constraint.
props.body: Check the absence against the policy's accrual and eligibility rules; flag mismatches.
props.sparkLine: Same policy, same report, every time.

beats.narration_text: Claude isn't approving the leave — it's running a written list, one item at a time, checking your request against the accrual, the eligibility window, and the blackout dates. Same policy in, same report out, every time. Approving is still yours.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I want to know whether a leave request will pass my company's PTO policy. Here's the request — paste the dates, the type of leave, and my remaining balance. Here's the policy — paste the accrual rules, the eligibility windows, and the blackout dates from the handbook. Walk me through it step by step. Does my accrued balance cover the requested days? Am I inside the eligibility window? Do any of the requested dates fall on a blackout date? If anything doesn't fit, tell me exactly which rule it fails and why. Show your reasoning; don't just give me a yes or no. Go deeper: ask the same model to draft three edge-case leave requests that look valid on paper but each fail a different rule — accrual, eligibility, or blackout — and name the tell in each one.
